newsitem.title: USA: Fourth Iditarod dog death stirs controversy.
newsitem.headline: Fourth Iditarod dog death stirs controversy.

text.p: The death of a fourth dog in the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race has renewed criticism of the event as too dangerous for the animals.

"The basic point is that these dogs are being pushed beyond their physical limits. And there are very few indicators for mushers to know that the dogs are in trouble," Wayne Pacelle, a vice president of the Humane Society of the United States, said Friday.
Pacelle said the deaths of the dogs "should raise many red flags and should cause substantive action, other than just the usual rhetoric."
His organisation wants the 1,161-mile (1,870 km) Anchorage-to-Nome race shortened, rearranged into stages and changed in other ways, Pacelle said.

The Iditarod has never been run without a dog death, but such occurrences have been limited to one or two animals a race in recent years. Iditarod officials and top mushers have said they cannot explain this year's fatalities.
Past criticism by the national Humane Society and other animal-welfare groups has cost the Iditarod several national sponsors.
But new backers have replaced old sponsors, and the race budget recovered enough this year to offer a total prize purse of over $400,000, up from last year's $300,000.
Meanwhile two-time champion Martin Buser surged to the lead on Friday, overtaking past champions Jeff King and Doug Swingley.

Buser departed Shageluk, an Athabaskan Indian village 629 miles (1,010 km) into the race course, at 6:41 a.m. (10:41 a.m. EST). He was followed 86 minutes later by Swingley, who won the 1995 race and set the course record of nine days, two hours and 42:19 minutes.

King, also a two-time champion, departed the abandoned mining town of Iditarod -- the race's halfway point -- just before midnight but was not reported to have completed the 65-mile (104 km) run to Shageluk Friday morning.
Of the 53 mushers who began the race Saturday, three have dropped out.
